text: Welcome to Time Series and Financial Modeling, step five of the Quantitative Developer path. Almost every model you'll build in this course sits on top of one basic transformation: turning prices into returns. Get that step wrong, and everything downstream inherits the mistake.

Raw prices are non-stationary — their mean and variance drift over time — so we model returns instead. Simple returns, price now over price before minus one, are cross-sectionally additive: a portfolio's return is just the weighted average of its holdings' simple returns. Log returns, the natural log of that same ratio, are time additive instead: the return over several periods is simply the sum of the one-period log returns. That's why nearly every model later in this course is written in terms of log returns.

In pandas, pct_change on a price series gives you simple returns directly. For log returns, take the natural log of the price series first, then difference it — numpy's log, followed by pandas diff. Both leave the first observation as NaN, since there's no prior price to compare against, so drop it before fitting anything.

Here's where the two diverge in practice. Log returns compound by simple addition — sum them up, then exponentiate to recover cumulative growth. Simple returns compound multiplicatively — one plus each return, multiplied together. A beginner mistake is summing simple returns directly across many periods; that overstates true compounding almost immediately.

Hold onto the distinction: simple returns add across assets, log returns add across time. Next lesson, we look at why the raw closing price straight from an exchange is usually the wrong number to feed into any of this in the first place.
